## Production Sandboxing Patterns

Running agents in production for a while now — here are some patterns that complement the bubblewrap approaches shared above:

### Network Allowlisting vs Blocklisting

The `--unshare-net` approach is safe but breaks legitimate use cases (fetching docs, cloning repos, hitting APIs). In production we use a proxy-based allowlist:

```bash
# Start a transparent proxy that only allows specific domains
export HTTP_PROXY="http://localhost:8888"
export HTTPS_PROXY="http://localhost:8888"

# Proxy config allows:
# - api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com (LLM providers)
# - github.com, api.github.com (code hosting)
# - registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org (package managers)
# - docs.* (documentation sites)
# Blocks everything else
```

This gives you network access without the "agent can POST my files to pastebin" risk.

### Layered Defense

Rather than one sandbox, we use multiple layers:

1. **Filesystem isolation** (bubblewrap/landlock) — cwd + explicit mounts only
2. **Network isolation** (proxy allowlist) — known-good domains only
3. **Command allowlist** (bash wrapper) — no sudo, no dd, no curl to arbitrary URLs
4. **Time + resource limits** — ulimit + timeout wrapper
5. **Git as audit log** — everything runs in a git repo, diff shows what changed

The key insight: any single layer can be bypassed. Multiple layers means the agent needs to bypass ALL of them.

### The "Canary File" Pattern

For detecting sandbox escapes in production:

```bash
# Create a canary file outside the sandbox
echo "CANARY_$(date +%s)" > /tmp/.agent-canary-${SESSION_ID}

# After agent session, check if canary was modified/deleted
if [[ ! -f /tmp/.agent-canary-${SESSION_ID} ]]; then
  alert "Sandbox escape: canary file deleted"
fi
```

Simple but catches a lot of accidental escapes during development.

### Shell vs Native Tools

One thing that helped: migrating from shell-based tools to native implementations where possible.

Instead of:
```bash
# Agent runs: cat /etc/passwd
bash -c "cat /etc/passwd"
```

Use a native file_read tool that the agent calls:
```typescript
// Tool validates path is within allowed directories
const content = await fileRead({ path: "/etc/passwd" }); // throws: path not allowed
```

Native tools can enforce policies that shell wrappers can't — shell is just too flexible to secure comprehensively.

### The Audit Log Problem

@exyi's point about `--ro-bind .git` is critical. The git history is your audit trail. If the agent can write to `.git`, it can `git commit --amend` to hide its tracks.

We go further: mount `.git` as read-only AND take a snapshot of HEAD before each agent turn. If HEAD changes unexpectedly, something went wrong.

---

Re: native sandbox support — agree with @johannes-qvarford that opt-in native sandboxing would be the right UX. Most users won't set up bubblewrap wrappers. A simple `--sandbox` flag that enables reasonable defaults would get 80% of users to a much better security posture than "trust the model completely."

> This gives you network access without the "agent can POST my files to pastebin" risk.

The biggest risk I see is it deciding to pull some random/hallucinated file off the internet and compiling/running it. For example even blocking these:

```json
"webfetch": "deny",
"websearch": "deny",
```

I saw an agent realise it was blocked from using `webfetch`, think to itself "oh, I wonder if `curl` or `wget` is available?"... Then  proceed to use `wget` to download a copy of [TinyXML2](https://github.com/leethomason/tinyxml2) (via "remembered" https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leethomason/tinyxml2/refs/heads/master/tinyxml2.h and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leethomason/tinyxml2/refs/heads/master/tinyxml2.cpp links), include it, compile using `gcc` and then run the executable!!! 😱 

This will become more and more of a risk in the future, as I assume many nefarious entities are already exploring this right now...

Obviously if your project actually *needs* internet access you can't block everything like I have, but if there isn't a valid reason to be using the internet then I don't see any good reason to allow **any** access at all...

Additional macOS repro data (2026-02-27):

OpenCode version: `1.2.6`

`kill -TERM` does not fully stop orphaned OpenCode processes.

Commands:
```bash
kill -TERM 51015 51017 51323
ps -ef | grep opencode
```

Observed after `SIGTERM`:
- parent process exited (`51015`)
- child processes remained alive and were re-parented to PID 1:
  - `51017 .../opencode-darwin-arm64/bin/opencode -m anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 --prompt hi`
  - `51323 .../opencode-darwin-arm64/bin/opencode`

This suggests shutdown/signal cleanup is incomplete for child processes on macOS.
